Charlie Brown · practical care playbook

Find it. Catch it. Kill it. Prevent more.

One flea has been reported on Charlie. The date and treatment status are not confirmed. Use this hands-on guide to check both cats and document results.

01

Find the flea

Set Charlie on a white towel in bright light. Part fur around the neck, shoulders, belly, inner thighs and base of tail. Slowly pull a fine-tooth flea comb through to skin, then inspect the teeth.

Look for a tiny dark-brown, fast-moving insect, or pepper-like black specks. Place specks on a damp white paper towel; a reddish-brown stain suggests flea dirt (digested blood), not definitive confirmation.

02

Catch it before it jumps

Comb in short passes over the towel. Keep a small cup of water plus a few drops of dish soap nearby, safely away from the cat. Dip any flea caught in the comb straight into the cup, or press it between two pieces of clear tape.

Fleas jump quickly—avoid releasing the combed debris back into the fur. Save a taped specimen for the veterinarian if identification is uncertain.

03

Kill the captured flea

Fully submerge the flea in the dish-soap water; leave it submerged, then discard the water where the cats cannot reach it. Alternatively seal it securely inside folded transparent tape.

Do not bathe cats in dish soap or put insecticides, essential oils, alcohol or household sprays on their skin. Removing one flea does not mean the wider problem is resolved.

04

Check Louie and the environment

Repeat a careful flea-comb check on Louie. Wash the cats’ washable bedding, vacuum furniture, carpets, upholstery and crevices, then promptly dispose of vacuum debris outdoors. Continue checking for fleas, flea dirt, scratching and irritated skin.

Ask the veterinarian about an effective cat-specific prevention/treatment plan for both cats based on weight, age, health and other medications. Flea stages in the environment can require ongoing control.

Illustrated flea-finding procedureIllustrative guide using reference-inspired cats; not original photographs or a diagnosis. Use the written checklist for accurate steps.
CAT SAFETY: Never use dog-only flea treatments on cats, especially products containing permethrin. Do not use essential-oil remedies. If a cat shows tremors, drooling, seizures, weakness, or unusual symptoms after exposure, contact an emergency veterinarian immediately. A captured flea is not proof that either cat has received treatment.
